newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Pan-European growth stocks market set for launch.
newsitem.headline: Pan-European growth stocks market set for launch.

text.p: Europe sees the birth on Monday of Easdaq, a growth stocks market modelled on New York's Nasdaq, which promises to give start-up firms access to a wider range of capital than their national stock markets can provide.

But the Brussels bourse, involved in a rival "Euro Nouveau Marche" project in which individual bourses are setting up their own markets for small-capitalisation stocks, said only time would tell if both could flourish.
Based in Brussels, Easdaq (European Association of Securities Dealers Automated Quotation) will be a pan-European, quote-driven market based on screen trading.
"From Monday Easdaq will be available for trading, will have been tested and the legal structure will be in place," Easdaq executive Chris Pickles told Reuters.
However delays in translating the rules, which have been approved by Belgian finance minister Philippe Maystadt, meant it was unlikely any stocks would be traded on day one, he added.
Initially only stocks already on Nasdaq would be quoted.
"When the market starts it's going to take a couple of weeks to build up enough liquidity for IPOs (initial public offerings)," Pickles said.
Easdaq has an agreement with the successful Nasdaq exchange, where many European growth companies currently seek capital, to enable both markets to offer firms a dual trading facility.

Belgian bio-tech firm Innogenetics, 12.5 percent owned by Kredietbank, and Belgian-based software firm Artwork Systems, as well as Canada's Nasdaq-listed bio-tech firm DynaMotive have already said they will seek Easdaq listings.
To qualify, companies must have total assets of 3.5 million Ecus ($4.43 million) and capital and reserves of two million Ecus. They must also be supported by at least two market-makers.
Easdaq envisages it will be quoting 50 stocks in 12 months, mounting to 500 in five years, though its business plan does not foresee breakeven until the fourth year of operations.
The project originated from contacts between the European Venture Capital Association, European Commission and various market players, and Nasdaq is one of its 91 shareholders.
Olivier Lefebvre, head of the Brussels bourse management committee, told Reuters Easdaq was essentially a competitor to the federation-style Euro-NM project.

Paris set up its Nouveau Marche in February as part of the Euro-NM project while Brussels and Frankfurt are due to launch their "new markets" in 1997. Lefebvre said the Amsterdam bourse was also interested in joining the federation.
The bourse-promoted Euro-NM aims to interconnect its various markets, have an international marketing plan and harmonise its rules on market introductions.
"This bottom up approach is the best," Lefebvre said. It took account of the fact firms were well known on their home markets, and that was where their shares saw most liquidity.

"It is not bad to have the two initiatives - the more we have the quicker we can gather momentum (for growth stocks) in Europe," Lefebvre said. But "only time will tell" if there was enough interest to sustain both schemes.
Easdaq says it will let investors trade in shares without the costs associated with cross-border transactions.
Its traders are linked by a computer system modelled on TRAX, the International Securities Markets Association communications system, and deals will be settled by Switzerland's INTERSETTLE.

Such an exchange was made possible by the European Union's Second Banking Directive, Investment Services Directive and Prospectus Directive, which allow stock markets, brokers and companies to operate and to move capital throughout the Union without having to seek regulatory approval in each member state.

Easdaq's board of directors outlines general policy, while the first line market regulator is to be an independent and autonomous market authority which must be approved by the Belgian finance minister.
Second line regulator is the surveillance department of the Belgian Banking and Finance Commission which can in turn refer matters to the finance minister. ($1=.7907 Ecu)
